procedural_history.originating_court: Sub-Divisional Magistrate's Court (initially Kiraoli, then Kheragarh)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Kheragarh dated 5 June, 1965, forfeiting the surety bond of the appellant and directing the sum of Rs. 20,000 to be realised from the appellant as a fine.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a revision application in the High Court at Allahabad against the order of the Civil and Sessions Judge, Agra, dated 28 January, 1966, which had rejected the revision against the Magistrate's order. The High Court dismissed the revision application, finding no justification to reduce the amount of the bond and refusing to allow the appellant to raise the question of jurisdiction (that the bond was forfeited in a different court than where it was given) because it was not raised earlier.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment dated 17 May, 1968, of the Allahabad High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the High Court rightly refused the appellant permission to argue the ground of want of jurisdiction because it was interlaced with questions of fact and that the bond was to the court of the Magistrate, not a particular court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a plea of want of jurisdiction, on the ground that a surety bond was forfeited by a different court than the one in which it was executed, can be raised for the first time in the High Court.

facts: An appellant executed a surety bond in the court of a Sub-Divisional Magistrate, promising to produce a truck 'whenever ordered by the court'.
A different Sub-Divisional Magistrate in the same district ordered the appellant to produce the truck.
When the appellant failed to do so, the second Magistrate forfeited the bond.
The appellant did not challenge the jurisdiction of the second Magistrate's court before the Magistrate or the Sessions Judge.
For the first time, in his revision application to the High Court, the appellant argued that the bond could only be forfeited by the court in which it was originally executed.
law: A plea regarding a court's jurisdiction is considered 'interlaced with questions of fact' when its validity depends on factual circumstances, such as the transfer of a case, the abolition of a court, or a redistribution of judicial business.
Under Section 12 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a Magistrate exercises jurisdiction throughout the entire district.
The specific wording of a legal document, such as a surety bond, determines the obligations of the parties involved.
application: The Supreme Court first held that the High Court was correct to refuse to hear the jurisdictional plea because it was not raised in the lower courts.

The Court reasoned that such a plea depends on factual questions. Had the issue been raised earlier, facts could have been established regarding why a different court was handling the matter (e.g., the case might have been transferred, or court duties might have been reallocated). By failing to raise the issue, the appellant prevented these facts from being clarified.
The Court then provided a second, alternative reason based on the construction of the bond itself.

It found that the appellant's undertaking was to produce the truck 'whenever ordered by the court,' not by a *specific* court. The term 'the court' was interpreted to mean the Magistrate's court dealing with the case, which has jurisdiction over the whole district.
Therefore, an order from any Sub-Divisional Magistrate within that district was valid under the terms of the bond, and the second court did have the jurisdiction to forfeit it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's plea. It decided that a plea of want of jurisdiction, when it is tied to questions of fact, cannot be raised for the first time in the High Court. Furthermore, on a plain reading of the bond, the undertaking was to the Magistrate's court in general, not to a specific named court, making the forfeiture order valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether the undertaking in the surety bond to produce a truck 'whenever ordered by the court' restricted the power of forfeiture to the specific Magistrate's court where the bond was executed.

facts: The appellant executed a surety bond in the court of a Sub-Divisional Magistrate, binding himself to produce a truck "whenever ordered by the court".
A different Sub-Divisional Magistrate's court within the same district later ordered the appellant to produce the truck.
When the appellant failed to produce the truck, the second Magistrate's court forfeited the bond.
law: Under Section 12 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a Magistrate exercises jurisdiction over the entire district.
application: The Court construed the language of the bond, noting that the undertaking was to produce the truck "whenever ordered by the court," not in a specific, named court.
The Court interpreted the word "court" in the bond to mean the Magistrate's court that was dealing with the case at the time, not the specific Magistrate who initially accepted the bond.

Since a Magistrate's jurisdiction covers the whole district, the undertaking was made to the magisterial court of the district, allowing any competent Magistrate within that district handling the case to enforce the bond.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the bond's language did not restrict the power of forfeiture to the specific court where it was executed. The undertaking was to the Magistrate's court of the district, and any Magistrate handling the case within that district had the authority to order the production of the truck and forfeit the bond.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a plea of want of jurisdiction, on the ground that a surety bond was forfeited by a different court than the one in which it was executed, can be raised for the first time in the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The surety bond was executed in the court of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Kiraoli, but was forfeited by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Kheragarh, who lacked jurisdiction to do so.
respondent_arguments: The plea of jurisdiction should not be allowed to be raised for the first time in the High Court as it was not raised before the Magistrate or the Sessions Judge.

Such a plea is interlaced with questions of fact, such as whether the case was transferred, a court was abolished, or business was reallocated, which could have been clarified if the issue was raised earlier.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the undertaking in the surety bond to produce a truck 'whenever ordered by the court' restricted the power of forfeiture to the specific Magistrate's court where the bond was executed.
appellant_arguments: The undertaking to produce the truck 'whenever ordered by the court' referred specifically to the court where the bond was executed (Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Kiraoli), and no other court.
respondent_arguments: The language of the bond did not specify an undertaking to produce the truck in a particular court; the undertaking was general.
The term 'court' in the bond refers to the Magistrate's court dealing with the case, and a Magistrate exercises jurisdiction over the whole district.
The undertaking was to the 'court of the Magistrate', not a specific named court.

cases.principle: This case was explicitly 'held inapplicable' by the Supreme Court and was therefore not relied upon.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A plea regarding a court's lack of jurisdiction cannot be raised for the first time in a higher appellate court if the plea is dependent on questions of fact that were not established in the lower courts.
obiter: When a surety bond requires an action 'whenever ordered by the court' without naming a specific court, the undertaking is to the Magistrate's court that is handling the case at the relevant time.
The term 'court' in a surety bond can mean the Magistrate's court in general, as a Magistrate exercises jurisdiction throughout the entire district.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that a plea of want of jurisdiction cannot be raised for the first time in the High Court when it is interlaced with questions of fact that could have been clarified if the issue had been raised in the lower courts. Furthermore, even on a pure construction of the surety bond, the undertaking to produce the truck "whenever ordered by the court" was a general obligation to the Magistrate's court as an institution dealing with the case, not to a specific, named court, and therefore the forfeiture by a different Magistrate's court in the same district was valid.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a plea of jurisdiction is interlaced with questions of fact, which would preclude it from being raised for the first time at a late appellate stage.
Construction of the language of a surety bond to determine the scope of the undertaking, specifically interpreting the meaning of the word 'court'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant was procedurally barred from raising the jurisdiction issue because it had not been raised before the Magistrate or the Sessions Judge.

The plea of jurisdiction was deemed to be 'interlaced with questions of fact,' such as whether the case was transferred, a court was abolished, or business was reallocated, which could only have been clarified if the point was urged at the proper time.
On construction of the bond, the court found 'there was no undertaking to produce the truck in a particular court.' The undertaking was general.
The court interpreted the word 'court' in the bond to 'mean the Magistrate's court which dealt with the case,' not the specific court where the bond was executed.
why_respondent_won: The High Court was correct to refuse the appellant permission to raise the jurisdiction ground for the first time on appeal.
The court accepted the argument that the jurisdiction plea depended on facts that were not on the record because the issue was not raised earlier.
The court accepted that the undertaking in the bond was general, as the appellant 'bound himself to produce the truck whenever ordered by the court to produce the same.'

The court reasoned that 'the Magistrate exercises jurisdiction in the whole district under s. 12 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,' supporting the view that the undertaking was to the Magistrate's court as an institution within that district.
policy_considerations: A party cannot be permitted to raise a plea for the first time at a high appellate stage if it is mixed with factual questions, because the opposing party and the court are deprived of the opportunity to elucidate the relevant facts at the trial level.
